**Solution 1 (√5−1)/2 ≈ 0.618: REJECT.** Take a set S with |S| = n+1, split evenly as n/3 in each class, and forbid every triple with at least two vertices in S. A perfect matching would need each edge to contain at most one S-vertex, so it covers at most n vertices of S, which is impossible. For v in S, the link is K_{2n/3,2n/3}, with spectral radius 2n/3. For v outside S, the link is K_{n,n} minus K_{n/3,n/3}, which has larger spectral radius. So every link has spectral radius at least about 2n/3 > 0.618n, and c ≥ 2/3 > (√5−1)/2. The claimed upper bound is refuted.

**Solution 2 1/2: REJECT.** The same construction gives spectral radius about 2n/3 at every vertex with no perfect matching. So c cannot be below 2/3, and 1/2 fails. The appeal to a "Dirac threshold" is also not a valid spectral argument.

**Solution 3 √((5+√17)/18) ≈ 0.7119: REJECT.** The computation of MMᵀ is wrong. In its construction, a row indexed by a vertex in A₂ has only n/3 ones, not 2n/3, so the entries 2n²/9 are incorrect. Redoing the block quotient gives the matrix (n²/9)[[2,1],[2,3]] with eigenvalues 4n²/9 and n²/9. So the spectral radius of that link is 2n/3, not the stated value. The value 0.7119 therefore has no support from the construction, and the claim that it is the threshold is unjustified.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
